title: A faint progenitor system for the faint Iax supernova 2024vjm - Nature Astronomy
byline: Zimmerman; Erez A; Gal-Yam; Avishay; Groot; Paul J; Ofek; Eran O; Roestel; Jan van; Pastorello; Andrea; Valenti; Stefano; Ravi; Aravind P; Chen; Ping; Schulze;
html:
Abstract

Type Ia supernovae are famous for their role as standardized cosmological candles. Their uniformity is attributed to their single origin: thermonuclear explosions of white dwarf stars. Nevertheless, some type Ia supernovae break this regularity. Prominently, the Iax subclass are less energetic and diverse, raising questions about their progenitor channel. A luminous blue star was identified in pre-explosion images of the bright type Iax SN 2012Z, in line with deflagration models of a white dwarf in which the star is not fully disrupted. However, these models fail to explain the properties of the faintest type Iax explosions, suggesting a possible different progenitor channel for faint events. Here we present the faint type Iax supernova SN 2024vjm, possibly the faintest supernova observed to date. Using a deep pre-explosion image from the Euclid space mission, we show that its progenitor system must be fainter than any previous Iax candidate progenitor system. Our limits also provide strong arguments against a massive-star origin. Our observations show that the slowly expanding ejecta of the supernova remain denser than those of bright Iax supernovae. We suggest that this leads faint type Iax supernovae to fade more slowly than bright ones, that is, in the opposite manner from the famous Phillips relation.

Data availability

Photometry and spectra used in this study are available via WISeREP106. A log of the available spectra can be found in Supplementary Table 1. The JWST data used for this study are available via MAST at https://doi.org/10.17909/m3aj-1c81 (ref. 107). The Euclid ERO used for this study are available from the ESA at https://doi.org/10.57780/esa-qmocze3 (ref. 11). Very Large Telescope/MUSE data are available from the ESO archive.

Code availability

The scripts used for the analyses presented in this paper are available via GitHub at https://github.com/erezimm/SN2024vjm. The analysis was performed in Python using NumPy108, SciPy109, Astropy110,111, pandas112, Matplotlib113 and extinction114. The light-curve interpolation used scikit-learn86. The forced PSF photometry on the Euclid image used Photutils75. The precision astrometry used AstroPack/MAATv266,67 and catsHTM68. The MUSE data cube was sky-subtracted with ZAP115 and analysed with MPDAF116. The stellar evolution tracks are from BPASS v2.2.118,19.
